Debate: Should Libertarians Support Rand Paul?

I agree with Ostrowski:

Rand has denied being a libertarian. Worse yet, he has described the term as an “albatross” around his neck ...[M]y concern is that Rand will become an albatross around the neck of the Liberty Movement.

What do others here think?

That's definitely a damning statement, but what does it really mean? We know that Rand is definitely not a libertarian, but he's the closest the mainstream parties will produce that have a chance at winning. Rand said that to sway Republican voters, to show that he isn't as "insane" as his father is/was. It's a fact that libertarians do not have nearly the voting power as the average conservative. If Rand has decent policies, which I think he does for now, but says rhetoric like that, then I think we should give him a good chance. It's just rhetoric. Focus on the policies.

Rand Paul is not the best libertarian candidate. However, he is the best possible candidate to inject libertarian ideas and philosophies into the next presidential election. When given the opportunity, I normally choose the Libertarian candidate over the parties, but I will support and vote for Rand Paul just like I did his father.

It does seem like a good strategy at this point. I've had a hard time coming to terms with this because I've traditionally disagreed with the lesser-of-two-evils argument. I still wonder to myself what the difference here is or why I'm okay with this hypocrisy. Maybe there is some kind of a balance between how much a politician's rhetoric represents someone and how likely they are to be able to represent that someone in government.
My view is that on the scale of libertarian to authoritarian, the Ds and Rs average around 60% towards authoritarian. Rand maybe a 40%. Best person with any chance of winning.

Generally speaking, I perceive little difference between R's and D's. The choice is similar to that between Coke or Pepsi -- little difference in taste and both will kill you in the long run.

It would be a breath of fresh air to see a true debate of ideas in the electoral process. I would welcome a contest between say Rand and Bernie. Now that would be a debate.

Assuming that we end up with a 'choice' of Clinton or Bush, I will vote for the Libertarian Party candidate. [When I wrote that it occurred to me that we could have a lot of fun with that pairing -- Vote for Clinton's Bush. Perhaps I'll secretly hope for that...]

While I agree with Ostrowski's thesis that we should pursue alternatives, I find the argument not to vote abhorrent. There is no better way to cede control than by allowing 'them' to choose for us.

I am afraid that his policies on gay marriage and other conservative rocks will be like Rothbard's pandering to racists in the south in the 60's. I don't think Rothbard was a racist at all but him and Ron Paul made libertarianism palatable to people with those beliefs and damned us all as racist segregationists despite libertarianism being the most progressive of all parties.

Yes.

Too often libertarians make the perfect the enemy of the good. They are happy to lose with pure principles instead of win a partial victory. That approach doesn't work in a democracy. It only works in dictatorships and only for the dictator. Sadly, not everyone agrees with us (for that matter WE don't always agree with us). Nobody of any political persuasion can get to 50%+1 of the vote with only those who agree with them on all particulars. To influence policy you have to work for gradual change, winning partial victories you can build on later, and be willing partners within larger coalitions of people you don't fully agree with. I'd rather see a libertarian caucus within one or both of the major parties made up of elected politicians who actually influence policy than an endless series of candidates I agree with 99% of the time in theory but who never get above single digits at the polls.

I've been asking myself this question for a while now, but there is a question directly related to this that no one is asking. With Paul running how is it(or will be) hurting the actual Libertarian Party itself?

If Paul wins the Republican Nomination he will draw votes from people who would normally vote Libertarian due to the fact that he is the closest Republican to Libertarian ideals(some might even argue that he is a Libertarian disguising himself as a Republican for election purposes, but I'll leave that debate for another day). With that it would actually hurt the Libertarian Party itself because votes would not be casted for the Libertarian Party nominee(lets say for argument sake Gary Johnson wins nomination again) as some would vote for Paul. This makes 2016 a bad year for the Libertarian Party coming off the heels from the great turnout in 2012.

On the flipside of the coin, say Paul does not win the nomination and a more traditional Republican wins nomination ( for argument sake lets say Mike Huckabee wins), but Paul's message of liberty is still spread. With that people might look for a party/candidate who is similar in ideals in sharp contrast to Huckabee. The Libertarian Party could pick up extra votes from Paul supporters who found the Libertarian Party due to his Libertarian views. This could make 2016 a great year for the Libertarian Party.

The third set up is very similar to the last one only with one little change(though it is the least likely). Recall in 2012 Johnson originally ran for the Republican Party and when he pulled out of the race he went to the Libertarian Party becoming its nominee(being one of the most successful Libertarian Presidential Nominees). What if Paul loses Republican nomination to a more traditional Republican(again Huckabee for this set up) and he decides to do what Johnson did in 2012: run for Libertarian nomination. The major question is would Paul change his senate affiliation with the Republican Party to the Libertarian Party. Not necessarily, he might take some flack from his fellow members, but not be expelled from the Party itself. Paul is to powerful in the Party to be thrown out. Just remember in this election Sanders is a Independent(who really is a member of the Vermont Progressive Party) running for Democratic nomination so stranger nominations have happened. But digressing back to the point, with supporters from his Republican Party and the Libertarian Party ticket he could make serious waves possibly breaking the 2 party system by passing 5% of the vote and granting the Libertarian Party major party status.

Candidly, fuck Rand Paul. He has shown time and again that he can't be trusted and he's far too weak a supported of liberty-centric values. Unless there are no other candidates (which is impossible), my principles dictate he cannot get my vote.
with Julian Assange calling him "America's last hope", I have to at least take him seriously. Rand Paul will get my vote if he gets the nomination

Most cultures have a unique building syle. When you see a building, you'll usually know immediately where it's from. What are some building styles in your world?
What is the architecture in your world like?

The lands of the Hirzam have very little good-quality wood available, and fires inspire a looming dread in the locals, hesitant to forget which swath of cropland and homes and folk was last lain to ash. To keep themselves from the perils of exposure, the Hirzam cobble their homes of stone, using both uncut rocks and adequately-hewn bricks as the purpose suits. And they do the same to wall their fields, not just to mark where one man's property gives way to the next, but also in the hope of keeping cropfires at bay, like a stout castle holds back a horde of reavers.

The Hirzam are not so skilled in quarrying as their southern neighbors, and so rarely do they use large slabs in any of their constructs. However, when they do use these, they carve grooves all along their surface, such that any blaze that might reach the constructed wall may not crack and destroy it, no matter how hatefully it licks it. These grooves are often lain out in the ornate, flowery designs of which the Hirzam are known for; The exception is upon buildings of governance and other import, where these grooves lie staunchly vertical. This is to prevent any villain with designs of entry from climbing too easily his target's wall. These vertical grooves have been called a requisite for all government buildings for some time now. It is said that this began after a particularly disastrous breach, although the histories do not agree upon its details.

And so it is that when a traveler in Hirzam comes upon a building of large, vertically grooved slabs, he may think "Ah! Here is home to some governance!"

Stone Structures

Massive stone structures can be found in every city, built in wide, squat pillars and walls to last for aeons.

These structures have stood for so long that their builders, their names, their original purposes, all have been lost to time. The only thing that remains are the stones themselves, set in strange recursing geometric patterns of spirals and shields. Every structure is set upon deep bedrock and made from a dark gray stone of great strength - they have endured wars and earthquakes, yet no broken structure has ever been found.

The most common structure is a tall obelisk, regularly patterned with holes, and buttresses extending outward to become walls that extend for the height of the obelisk, gradually dropping in height until they disappear. These structures can be found in sizes ranging from a man's height (these are simply ornamental or are used as anchors) to hundreds of meters tall. These structures are ordered around each other, with the largest being at the city center and smaller ones radiating outward.

(The best example I can imagine would be a combination of the ribs on the underside of a mushroom plus a crop circle all built by dwarven masons and older than prehistory. Then imagine, instead of ruins, an entire city of people living within these structures.)

Purpose

Many of the larger structures are unique, however, and seem to be designed for some kind of purpose. The central structure of Polis Agra, for example, features a large open ring about 100 m in diameter filled with clear fresh water. It is the only thing that allows the city to exist - Polis Agra is a desert city, yet it irrigates and harvests hundreds of acres around it. Any attempts to dig wells result in only dry bedrock or brackish salt water, which leaves the origin of Polis Agra's central water source a mystery.

In other cases, these purposes are not quite so clear. The city of Halishaft is built upon a series of open vertical circular shafts which extend deep into the ground. They are not mineshafts, for each one is lined in the structures' same polished stone all the way to the bottom. All but the largest shaft ends in a flat bottom, but the centermost shaft (nearly 10m wide) extends down farther than any have explored. Countless brave adventurers have ventured down, but few return - lending the city a certain kind of eerie reputation. The shaft is currently used as a refuse pit and is considered to be bottomless.

Modern Additions

The architecture itself is blunt and brutalist, with no defining marks or inscriptions, but the city dwellers have expanded upon these structures with wooden beams, rope and canvas awnings stretching to create shade and divide large spaces into smaller ones. It is usually considered crass to obstruct these structures' natural beauty, but sometimes necessity requires modification.

In many places the stones are painted to mark directions or ownership, however any attempts to scratch or carve on the stone is fruitless. A chiseler could work all day and barely mar the polished surface. Not that you could get away with it - anyone who defaces or alters a stone structure is harshly punished.
